description: Pilot: nonredundant, source-grounded point-of-reading clarifications. No chapter prose is replaced.

companions.passage: Russell initially described analysis as finding simpler elements within a complex claim.
companions.title: What does Russell mean by analysis?
companions.explanation: Russell tries to understand a complicated statement by examining its simpler parts and how they fit together. Moran introduces this as an early method of analytic philosophy. Later thinkers change the method, so this is a starting point rather than the definition of the entire tradition.

companions.passage: Singer extends moral consideration to sentient animals, while Parfit asks us to consider
companions.title: Why Parfit also questions our future selves
companions.explanation: Stout connects Parfit's concern for people not yet born with his view of personal identity. Our future selves, on this account, may be psychologically connected to us without being strictly the same person. That makes concern for future interests a wider question than simply protecting one's present self.
companions.added_value: Explains the personal-identity argument behind the future-generation discussion, which is absent from the short main-body account.

companions.passage: Hare distinguishes ordinary rule-following from critical calculation; rule-utilitarianism combines a generalization principle with a utilitarian way of selecting rules, though critics question whether it collapses into act-utilitarianism.
companions.title: What is borrowed from Kant?
companions.explanation: Stout explains that Harrod combines two ideas: a Kantian-style reason to follow general rules, and a utilitarian method for deciding which rules would have the best consequences. Utility helps select the rules, but does not by itself explain why we must always act by rules.
companions.added_value: Identifies the independent Kantian source of the rule-obligation premise, rather than repeating the existing definition of rule-utilitarianism.

companions.passage: while Kantian and phenomenological thinkers continued to ask how an objective world can be known by a subject.
companions.title: What is naturalism doing in this discussion?
companions.explanation: Naturalism looks mainly to nature and the sciences when explaining how things work. Moran contrasts its growing influence with philosophers who also ask how our knowledge can be objective. He is comparing approaches to a shared question, not changing the subject.

companions.passage: Around 1900, Freud's work,
companions.title: Why does Freud appear among philosophers?
companions.explanation: Moran is pointing to different intellectual beginnings around 1900. Their effects were not all the same. Freud represents a major new way of thinking about the mind, while the other names in this paragraph mark developments in logic and philosophy. This is a historical overview, not a list of one school.

companions.passage: Husserl opposed psychologism and developed phenomenology as a description of what appears to consciousness.
companions.title: What does phenomenological description mean here?
companions.explanation: Husserl asks us to describe carefully how something appears in conscious experience before forcing it into an explanation. Moran uses this method to show another influential route into questions about knowledge. Husserl and Frege both cared about logic and objectivity, even though their methods developed differently.

companions.passage: Quine attacked the analytic–synthetic distinction and argued that our beliefs meet experience as an interconnected body, not one statement at a time.
companions.title: Which distinction did Quine challenge?
companions.explanation: The analytic–synthetic distinction separates truths said to depend on meaning from truths said to depend on how the world is. Quine questions whether this neat separation holds. Moran includes him to show that analytic philosophy revised some of its own earlier assumptions.

companions.remember: Quine challenged a familiar boundary between kinds of truth.

companions.passage: Husserl, Patočka, Derrida, and Habermas debated its intellectual inheritance and the limits of European identity.
companions.text: Europe itself became a philosophical question
companions.title: Why is Europe a philosophical question?
companions.explanation: Here 'Europe' means more than a place on a map. Philosophers also argue about the ideas and traditions associated with it. Moran has been discussing wars, migration and changing intellectual centres. He now asks how that history changes the way philosophers understand Europe's identity.

companions.passage: He proposed testing and revising moral principles through reflection and practice.
companions.title: Dewey's weaker and stronger claims about constructing value
companions.explanation: Stout distinguishes a weaker view, where describing and working through a situation shapes which moral questions arise, from a stronger view, where rational experimentation actually makes the outcome good. He is cautious about attributing this stronger anti-realist claim to Dewey himself.
companions.added_value: Preserves Stout's explicit source qualification about Dewey rather than presenting constructivism as categorical.

companions.passage: Stout examines more reductive accounts, including Perry's treatment of value as an object of interest, as well as ideal-observer theories, relativism, and later Cornell realism.
companions.title: What the ideal observer is meant to explain
companions.explanation: Roderick Firth proposed interpreting an ethical judgment through how a fully informed, disinterested, consistent observer would respond. Stout uses Moore's challenge to ask why that observer's reaction should settle what I ought to do. Brandt developed a related but differently qualified account.
companions.added_value: Gives the specific mechanism and criticism of an approach otherwise only named.

companions.passage: Peter Geach also asks how a moral statement can keep its meaning inside an “if … then” argument.
companions.title: The problem of moral words inside logic
companions.explanation: Calling stealing wrong may seem like expressing disapproval. But in the statement 'If stealing is wrong, then …,' the speaker is not straightforwardly disapproving of stealing. Geach asks how the expression can still play the same logical role in an argument; Blackburn tried to answer through commitments between attitudes.
companions.added_value: Explains the embedded-statement problem and source response without duplicating the main text.

companions.passage: John Mackie's error theory argues that ordinary moral judgments claim an objective authority that the world does not provide.
companions.title: Why Mackie called objective values 'queer'
companions.explanation: Stout describes two parts of Mackie's challenge. Objective values would be unusual things in the world, and knowing them would require an equally unusual way of detecting them. Mackie therefore held that ordinary moral judgments claim more objectivity than exists and are, strictly speaking, false.
companions.added_value: Restores the separate metaphysical and epistemological reasoning behind Mackie's conclusion.

companions.passage: Sidgwick and Moore appealed to fundamental intuitive principles.
companions.title: Sidgwick's stages of intuitionism
companions.explanation: Stout reports Sidgwick's movement from judgments about particular cases, to intuitive rules, to deeper philosophical principles that cannot themselves be derived from still deeper rules. Stout then asks why these final principles should escape further justification and finds Sidgwick's preference for maximizing good open to challenge.
companions.added_value: Adds the sequence and Stout's challenge, not just a generic description of intuition.

companions.passage: These duties can conflict, leaving particular decisions less than certain.
companions.title: Why Ross does not offer a simple checklist
companions.explanation: Ross named duties such as fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, and avoiding harm. Their weight can differ by case, and consequences may be uncertain. Stout emphasizes that recognizing each duty intuitively does not mean that its final priority in a difficult situation is equally obvious.
companions.added_value: Gives the full source list and the distinction between identifying duties and judging an all-things-considered action.

companions.passage: The Prisoners' Dilemma shows why self-interest alone can undermine cooperative rules.
companions.title: Why individual advantage can defeat collective advantage
companions.explanation: Stout's problem is that everyone may be better off under shared rules, yet an individual can gain by breaking a rule while others obey it. If each person reasons that way, the system collapses. Gauthier responds by trying to build commitment into rational agency rather than treating every case as a fresh calculation.
companions.added_value: Shows the inferential step and Gauthier's response not included in the short note.

companions.passage: Scanlon, Rawls, and Habermas developed approaches grounded in agreements that reasonable people could accept.
companions.title: Three different forms of justified agreement
companions.explanation: Stout distinguishes Scanlon's question about rules no one could reasonably reject, Rawls's imagined agreement behind a veil of ignorance about one's place in society, and Habermas's inclusive discussion in which participants respect each other's viewpoints. All use agreement, but not in the same way.
companions.added_value: Restores differences between three theories presently grouped in one sentence.

companions.passage: Frege helped establish the precise logical treatment of statements and meanings.
companions.title: What does Frege contribute to this story?
companions.explanation: Frege used precise logic to study how statements work, including forms that ordinary grammar may hide. Moran identifies this as a major foundation of twentieth-century philosophy. Frege's role here is to show a new tool for questions about language and thought.

companions.passage: The later opposition between analytic and Continental philosophy can obscure their shared origins.
companions.title: Why are analytic and Continental philosophy mentioned together?
companions.explanation: They are names for influential philosophical traditions, but they do not describe two completely separate groups. Moran explains that both faced some of the same older questions. Their later differences make more sense once those shared beginnings are understood.

companions.passage: Political philosophy became prominent again through writers such as Arendt and, later, Rawls.
companions.title: Why does political philosophy enter the history?
companions.explanation: Political philosophy asks about questions such as justice, government and how people should live together. Moran is showing how war, persecution and changes in academic life affected what philosophers studied. Political philosophy's growing prominence is part of that historical development.

companions.passage: Philosophy must also examine its own history: ideas, names, and inherited problems do not have fixed meanings outside the debates that formed them.
companions.text: Philosophy must also examine its own history
companions.title: Why must philosophy study its own past?
companions.explanation: A philosophical idea can be understood differently as later thinkers question or reinterpret it. Moran is warning against a history that simply lists winners, losers and dates. The changing meaning of ideas helps explain why philosophy's development is not one straight line.

companions.passage: Stout examines more reductive accounts, including Perry's treatment of value as an object of interest, as well as ideal-observer theories, relativism, and later Cornell realism.
companions.title: Being valued is not automatically being valuable
companions.explanation: Westermarck linked wrongness to a person's or community's inclination to disapprove. Perry linked an object's value to someone's taking an interest in it. Stout applies Moore's question to both: does disapproval establish wrongness, or does interest establish goodness? He also notes that Perry later appealed to harmony among interests when discussing overall value.
companions.added_value: Distinguishes Westermarck and Perry and illustrates the open question applied to each.

companions.passage: Stout examines more reductive accounts, including Perry's treatment of value as an object of interest, as well as ideal-observer theories, relativism, and later Cornell realism.
companions.title: Does a framework make an act right?
companions.explanation: Brandt connects ethical language to attitudes endorsed after informed, intelligent reflection. Harman interprets moral claims in relation to a community's framework of conventions and attitudes. Stout asks why an informed judge's endorsement, or acceptance within one's own framework, should settle whether an act is really right or wrong. That question remains open for the agent.
companions.added_value: Recovers distinct analyses by Brandt and Harman and Stout's common criticism.

companions.passage: The Cornell realists answer that moral properties may be natural, causally important features of reality.
companions.title: How the Cornell realists identify moral properties
companions.explanation: Boyd described moral properties as clusters of mutually supporting natural properties, rather than definitions based on one feature. Sturgeon argued that someone's badness or goodness might help explain judgments and actions. Stout asks how the natural cluster connected with a moral term can be shown to coincide with what a person would reach through rational moral reflection.
companions.added_value: Preserves Boyd's cluster and Sturgeon's explanatory criterion and remaining challenge.

companions.passage: W. D. Ross instead identified several prima facie duties, such as fidelity, gratitude, justice, and avoiding harm.
companions.title: Why plural duties mattered in medical ethics
companions.explanation: Stout connects Ross's approach to Beauchamp and Childress's four principles of medical ethics: autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice. They are distinct considerations that can guide decisions even when no single universal rule determines the answer. This is Stout's example of intuitionism's continuing practical influence.
companions.added_value: Adds the source's important application of plural duties.

companions.passage: Stout connects this approach with feminist care ethics, virtue theory, and Continental discussions of our responsibility to others.
companions.text: Continental discussions of our responsibility to others
companions.title: Buber, Levinas and Scheler on sensitivity
companions.explanation: Stout connects Murdoch's attentive moral perception with Buber's 'I–Thou' relation, where another person is not treated merely as an object. For Buber, responding to a particular person also bears on one's relation to God. Levinas develops an ethics of encountering the Other, while Scheler argues that emotional experience can disclose values. These are related approaches, not one identical theory.
companions.added_value: Explains three Continental versions of a related idea.

companions.passage: Stout also traces an alternative: Charles Taylor sees self-definition as open to reasoned revision, while existentialists understand radical choice as a deeper source of freedom.
companions.title: What Beauvoir means by the ambiguity of freedom
companions.explanation: Stout contrasts Taylor's rationally revisable self-definition with existentialist radical choice, where value arises from a free decision rather than guiding it from outside. Simone de Beauvoir valued freedom but observed a tension: choosing freely gives a situation meaning, while that settled meaning also limits future freedom. She called this tension ambiguity.
companions.added_value: Preserves Beauvoir's specific account of ambiguity.

companions.passage: Stout traces a shift from pleasure toward preference satisfaction, which influenced decision theory and public policy.
companions.title: Ramsey's measurements and Stout's challenge
companions.explanation: Ramsey showed how choices between outcomes could measure preferences and bets could estimate degrees of belief. This helped rational choice and later welfare calculations. Stout nevertheless questions treating preference-satisfaction as the whole of rationality: the fact that people choose what they want does not establish that whatever they want is what they ought to choose.
companions.added_value: Connects the method to policy and the source's stated criticism.

companions.passage: Further disagreement concerned whether responsibility requires originating our own causes or having been able to do otherwise.
companions.title: Why some philosophers defended agent causation
companions.explanation: Stout reports Taylor's worry that describing mental events as causes leaves out the agent's own role in acting. Chisholm claimed free will requires some events to be caused by an agent rather than by prior events. Other philosophers judged this metaphysically costly, while compatibilists argued that determinism need not remove freedom or responsibility.
companions.added_value: Explains the causal-origination requirement and competing responses.

companions.passage: Singer extends moral consideration to sentient animals, while Parfit asks us to consider future generations.
companions.title: Who counts according to Singer?
companions.explanation: Stout reports Singer's claim that all and only sentient beings count in overall-happiness calculations. On that principle, if a newborn has less capacity to feel pain than a cow, Singer gives more weight to the cow's well-being in that comparison. Stout also records Singer's qualification that other factors complicate the judgment in practice.
companions.added_value: Preserves the exact criterion and its qualification.

companions.passage: rule-utilitarianism combines a generalization principle with a utilitarian way of selecting rules, though critics question whether it collapses into act-utilitarianism.
companions.title: Why Smart and Lyons disagreed about rules
companions.explanation: Smart argued that the universally best rule might itself be 'always maximize utility in each case', making rule-utilitarianism collapse into act-utilitarianism. Lyons answered that some formulations escape this collapse, though they may be less plausible on other grounds. Stout presents this as a problem for justifying rules when immediate consequences point the other way.
companions.added_value: Preserves the source objection and qualified response.

companions.passage: His open question argument asks: even if something gives pleasure, can we still meaningfully ask whether it is good?
companions.title: Why an open question must be tested carefully
companions.explanation: Stout warns that knowing how to use a word does not always mean that its meaning is perfectly clear to us. A question may look open even when it concerns meaning itself. Moore's test must therefore be applied carefully rather than treating every question that sounds discussable as proof that a definition fails.
companions.added_value: Preserves the explicit methodological caution that the existing examination question asks students to explain.

companions.passage: Nozick's experience-machine example questions whether pleasant experience is all we value.
companions.title: What happens in Nozick's experience machine?
companions.explanation: Imagine a machine that could give you every feeling of having achieved what matters to you. You could feel that you had written a great book without actually writing it. If you would refuse the machine, Nozick takes that to suggest that real achievements matter to you, not only the pleasant experience of having them.
companions.added_value: Provides the decisive details of Nozick's supplied example, which the main note names but does not narrate.

companions.passage: Others tried to justify moral rules through self-interest, commitment, or rights.
companions.title: Three attempts to connect rationality and moral commitment
companions.explanation: Baier argued that moral reasons take account of others and override immediate self-interest, while still grounding their priority partly in self-interest; Toulmin appealed instead to harmony among interests. Gauthier argued that rational agency includes commitment, which can sustain cooperation despite a temptation to cheat. Gewirth argued that claiming rights for oneself while refusing others' comparable rights is irrational.
companions.added_value: Distinguishes four named proposals left hidden by the main note's grouping of self-interest, commitment and rights.

companions.passage: Moral perception joins reason and appropriately developed emotion.
companions.title: Foot's example: the word 'rude'
companions.explanation: Stout reports Philippa Foot's example of the word 'rude'. A person's behavior may meet familiar criteria for being rude, while the word also expresses disapproval. Someone unwilling to make that evaluation may have to decline to use the term itself. This is why a morally thick word cannot be treated as a purely neutral description.
companions.added_value: Adds Foot's concrete source example of descriptive and evaluative meaning beyond the nearby definition of thick terms.
